fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Empire of the Great Khan on the Grandest Maps", "body": "Chance opens with Joan Blaeu's 1662 Atlas Maior, an eleven volume set that cost about as much as a large house and was easily the most expensive book of its century, where the label Tartaria sive Magni Chami Imperium, the empire of the Great Khan, sprawls across Asia above an Oceanus Tartaricus. He grants that maps like this make the conspiracy feel true and calls its questions, who took Tartaria off the map and why, legitimate ones, while tossing out the claim that the Great Wall faces the wrong way, since it was built to be defended from either side."}, {"title": "Fomenko and the New Chronology", "body": "Chance traces the modern Tartaria story back to the Russian mathematician Anatoly Fomenko and Gleb Nosovsky, whose new chronology holds that the Horde was simply the regular Russian army, that Khan and Tsar were interchangeable, and that Tartar raids were punitive tax collection. Their deeper thesis is that Russia was the secret origin of modern civilization, which American believers rarely realize. Dylan counters with Friar John's thirteenth century account, where orda means the tent of Guyuk Khan, and with the slaughter of Kiev, and hears in the whole scheme a late Soviet mythology built to restore national pride."}, {"title": "Checking the Source Behind the Claim", "body": "Fomenko, leaning on A. A. Gordeev's History of the Cossacks, says a letter from the Hungarian king Bela IV to Pope Innocent IV proves Batu Khan's army was Russian led. Chance went and found the letter itself, and it simply lists Hungary's hostile neighbors, Russians, Cumans, Brodniks, Bulgarians, Bosnians and Germans, after the Tartars had devastated the kingdom. That fabricated support left him suspicious of everything else, though he credits one point: the Chora Monastery mosaic of Maria Palaiologina, Saint Mary of the Mongols, really does render Mongols with a word close to the Greek for great."}, {"title": "Old Maps as Mythology and Geography", "body": "Abraham Ortelius in 1570 says his Tartary takes in the Scythias of the ancients and ties Central Asian peoples to the lost tribes of Israel, while labeling Japan as Chryse, the golden island that Pliny and Pomponius Mela placed in the far east and that Mercator repeated in 1569. Marco Polo described a palace roofed in pure gold on an island he never visited. Jodocus Hondius in 1606 confesses that no one could truly describe so vast and unknown a realm, and Chance calls this blend of classical geography, biblical history and the sixteenth century world pure farrago."}, {"title": "A Name That Never Held Still", "body": "Dylan reminds listeners that Tartary carries the root of Tartarus, the abyss and a synonym for hell, and that Western chroniclers likened its people to demons and called their leader Satan, so the word became an arbitrary label for whoever threatened Europe. Chance's Tartary Atlas makes the drift visible, gathering travelogues such as Hayton's 1307 Flower of the Histories of the East and nearly ninety maps whose time dial shows the outline of Tartary shifting from map to map, while a 1701 Siberian map commissioned under Peter the Great writes Great Tartary across Russia's own territory."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Why was Tartaria erased from the map? Was the Tartarian Empire a lost civilization, a historical cover-up, or something else? Chance Garton and Dylan Saccoccio investigate Grand Tartary through original maps, translated Latin inscriptions, and the sources behind the modern Tartaria conspiracy theory.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In Inner Whirled 30, we examine maps by Ortelius, Hondius, and Blaeu from the golden age of European cartography. These elaborate atlases raise fascinating questions, but what does their fine print actually say? We also follow the erased-empire theory back to Anatoly Fomenko's New Chronology and check the historical evidence cited in his work. What connects Tartary, the Mongol Empire, and Russia? Do the original sources support the story circulating online?

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The 1771 Britannica Under Scrutiny", "body": "Chance opens the members' hour with the 1771 Encyclopaedia Britannica, the page social media reels wave around as proof of a concealed country. Its appendix table splits Tartary into Chinese, Independent and Muscovite rows, with Muscovite Tartary at three million square miles and a capital at Tobolsk, while Russia gets only a million. Yet the same volume heads its Siberia entry as Asiatic Russia and says the Kalmyk Tartars acknowledge themselves subject to the Empire of Russia. The Tartary entry itself names no ruler, no capital and no government, so Chance reads it as a region and its peoples rather than a nation."}, {"title": "According to Map", "body": "Fomenko cites a map of North America from the same encyclopedia and reads its blank northwest as the last remnant of the Horde resisting foreign explorers. The conversation catches that the map itself labels that country as parts undiscovered, so his phrase \"according to map\" claims far more than the map says. The hosts offer a plainer reading: by the late 1700s, standardized celestial navigation let explorers finish the maps of North America and Asia at the same time. Dylan adds that only 3 to 5 percent of Russians were literate by 1800, against 85 to 90 percent of Americans, so a war in America would have left letters."}, {"title": "Copying the Flag Charts", "body": "The claim that Tartary had its own flag gets a long look. Chance tracks the yellow owl and dragon banners from Pieter Schenk in 1711 through Johann Baptist Homann to Carington Bowles in 1783, while several of the books and charts tie the dragon flag to the Emperor of China. The oldest version he found sits in Carel Allard's flag book of about 1694, which seems to borrow a black owl coat of arms Pierre Duval invented in 1676 from a legend of an owl saving Genghis Khan. Dylan points to the surviving Spanish Armada flag of 1588 as proof that real flags of that era endure."}, {"title": "Nieuhof's Embassy and the Great Khan", "body": "Chance reads from Johan Nieuhof's account of the Dutch East India Company embassy to Peking, where the Great Khan of Tartary and the Emperor of China were the same man, Shunzhi of the Qing dynasty. The court puzzled over a Holland governed by councils instead of a king, the Jesuit Johann Adam Schall von Bell warned officials against the Dutch, and a Muscovite envoy was turned away for refusing to bow. Chance argues that if Russia and the Tartar Empire were one, Moscow could not have been denied, and that after the 1650s a Tartar empire in European sources usually means China."}, {"title": "Heads I Win, Tails You Lose", "body": "Chance lays out how Fomenko would answer: the Romanovs took the throne in 1613 with help from the Vatican and European powers, the empire broke into rival pieces by 1650, and Siberia stayed independent until the 1770s. Dylan objects that Kiev, not Moscow, was the major city in the accounts of the Khans. Chance then brings in Philip Johan von Strahlenberg, a Swede captured at Poltava in 1709 and held in Tobolsk from 1711 to 1721, and the 1689 Treaty of Nerchinsk setting a Russian and Chinese border inside Siberia. He calls the method heads I win, tails you lose, where any inconvenient document becomes a forgery."}]

It looks like Tartaria is the name of several different poorly defined regions.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "When you're talking about conflicts in America, to not have any letters from soldiers on those front lines writing to their loved ones is asinine.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I really did look for any sign that this spiral flag ever existed. So some of these flags should be in custody remaining somewhere.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "Until someone can provide a substantial piece of evidence, like a physical flag or something outside of these old flag charts that appear to be copy-pasta, I accept the explanations I've just given.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "In the Middle Ages, there's no accounts of them having standards or flags.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "We have a Tartar emperor ruling a vast empire, so there is a Tartarian empire. It's just not the one that the conspiracy theory is talking about.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "It would just be cool if people from those other countries could someday look at Western historical accounts and kind of correct them, or just show you what that person probably meant.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "If Russia and the Tartar Empire were one and the same, how is it that Moscovy, Moscow, would send an ambassador to the Tartar emperor and get denied?", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "If you find evidence that falsifies your idea and you keep finding evidence that falsifies it, you accept that your idea is wrong.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}]

So let's try to get some answers.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "It's pretty common that that part of the world was referred to as Tartaria, and people will ignore the fact that the root of it is Tartaros or Tartarus, which is the abyss or darkness or blackness, and it's also an allegory or a synonym for hell.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "We don't just read a book and take it for granted what they're telling us.
